activities.anchor: the atom or bond that does the chemistry
activities.caption: file each description under its family
activities.name: ochFamilySort

config.prompt: File each description under its family:

items.label: every carbon holds four neighbours, formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
a C=C double link, planar and electron-rich
burns; swaps in halogens only under UV light
strong, nonpolar links with no electron-poor sites

config.why: Learn one alkene reaction and you know ten thousand molecules' behaviour — the power of grouping by the reactive site.

activities.anchor: which is why gas heaters need ventilation
activities.caption: true or false — what the inert family actually does
activities.name: ochCombustJudge

statements.s: Complete combustion of methane gives CO₂ and H₂O: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.
statements.why: ΔH = −890 kJ/mol — the energy that powers kitchens, turbines and engines.

statements.s: Incomplete combustion makes carbon dioxide and water too, just less of each.
statements.why: Starved of oxygen it makes carbon MONOXIDE — the silent poison that binds haemoglobin 200× tighter than O₂ — plus soot.

statements.s: Under UV light an alkane substitutes: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl.
statements.why: Via a radical chain mechanism — famously catastrophic when radicals meet ozone (the CFC story).

statements.s: Alkanes react readily with ionic reagents because of their electron-poor sites.
statements.why: The opposite: strong nonpolar C–C and C–H bonds with nothing to grip — that absence IS the inertness.

activities.anchor: admit it to a tower that cools upward
activities.caption: slide to where the petrol band condenses
activities.name: ochPetrolPlace

config.prompt: Crude enters hot and sorts itself as it rises. Slide the marker to the top of petrol's condensation band.
config.why: Petrol is C₄–C₈, condensing at 40–100 °C; the bottled-gas band sits higher up, kerosene spans 150–240, and bitumen never leaves the bottom (over 350 °C).

activities.anchor: allegedly from a dream of a snake biting its tail
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the benzene puzzle
activities.name: ochBenzSpot

config.prompt: A student retells the benzene story. One line is wrong — click it:
lines: The 1865 hexagon got the geometry right, but not the stability.
Real benzene's six C–C links are all identical, 139 pm — between C–C's 154 and C=C's 134.
Its hydrogenation energy is about 150 kJ/mol less exothermic than three separate double links would predict.
The six extra electrons sit in three fixed alternating double links, exactly as the hexagon-with-three-double-lines symbol shows.
The lower-energy arrangement is why benzene is famously reluctant to react despite its formula.
config.correction: The six extra electrons delocalise around the ring in a continuous π cloud — aromaticity — so the circle-in-hexagon is the honest picture; fixed alternating links are simply wrong.
config.why: The delocalised arrangement sits lower in energy than any alternating structure — the puzzle took a century to solve.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — the classic test for unsaturation
activities.name: ochBromCloze

config.text: Bromine water is %%0%%, and it %%1%% on shaking with an alkene — the classic test for %%2%%.
config.hint: The C=C pinches open easily and adds the halogen across itself — instant colour loss.

activities.anchor: The reactivity contrast with alkanes is the subject's cleanest before/after
activities.caption: drag the divider across the family divide
activities.name: ochDivideCompare

config.prompt: Same two elements, one extra shared pair — drag the divider across the divide:

before.label: the saturated family
before.text: Inert workhorses: strong nonpolar links, nothing to grip — they burn and (under UV) substitute, and that is all.

after.label: the double-link family
after.text: Addition machines: hydrogenation spreads, hydration to ethanol, instant halogen tests, polymerisation into roughly 400 million tonnes of plastic a year.

config.why: One pair of electrons, four new industries — the C=C unit is planar, electron-rich, and pinches open easily.

activities.caption: call the isomer count for a twenty-carbon chain
activities.name: ochIsomerEst

config.prompt: A formula does not fix a molecule. Roughly how many structural isomers does C₂₀H₄₂ have?
config.why: 366,319 — which is why naming rules exist, and why structure, not just composition, decides behaviour.
config.context: C₄H₁₀ has just two: straight butane (bp −0.5 °C) and branched isobutane (bp −11.7 °C).
